canonicalExplanation.summary: `git log` **walks history**: it lists commits reachable from where you are, newest first. Filters narrow it down: a path (`-- parser.ts`), text in messages (`--grep`), text in the code (`-S "token"`), an author, or a date. `--oneline --graph --all` draws branches. `git show <commit>` then **inspects one commit**: its full hash, author, date, message and exact patch. None of these commands change anything. And careful: the **newest** commit touching a file is not necessarily the one that introduced a particular line; search for the line itself.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
The parser has started rejecting empty strings, and a learner wants to know which commit changed that. They look at the top of `git log`, blame the most recent commit, and are wrong: that commit only fixed a typo. A learner searches log for changes to parser.ts, selects a full commit identity, and uses show to inspect that commit's exact patch. In this lesson you'll locate and explain the commit that introduced a supplied change.

```predict
{"question": "Does running git log, git show or git log --graph ever change your repository?", "options": ["Sometimes, if you use filters", "Never: they only read history"], "answer": 1, "why": "They're read-only, so explore freely."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Selective staging and first commit** and **Commit messages and scope**.

sections.heading: The model: log walks history, show inspects one object
sections.body:
```bash
git log --oneline -- src/parser.ts          # commits touching this file.
git log -S "if (!input)" -- src/parser.ts  # commits that added or removed this text.
git log --grep "empty" --oneline            # search messages.
git log --oneline --graph --all -15         # branch shape.

git show 4c1e2f9                            # metadata + full patch.
git show --stat 4c1e2f9                     # just the files changed.
git rev-parse 4c1e2f9                       # the full 40-character identity.
```

| Question | Command |
|---|---|
| which commits touched this file? | `git log -- path`. |
| which commit added this text? | `git log -S "text"`. |
| what exactly did that commit do? | `git show <hash>`. |
| which commit last changed each line? | `git blame path`. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why record the full hash rather than 4c1e2f9 in a bug report?", "answer": "Short hashes can become ambiguous as a repository grows. The full identity always names exactly one commit."}
```

sections.heading: Newest isn't guilty

includes: Filter git log by path, message text and code text, and draw history with --graph.
Inspect one commit's metadata and patch with git show and record its full identity.

outcomes: Locate and explain the commit that introduced a supplied change.

examples.title: Who changed the parser?
examples.situation: A learner searches log for changes to parser.ts, selects a full commit identity, and uses show to inspect that commit's exact patch.
walkthrough: **Searches log for changes to parser.ts:** `git log -S "if (!input)" -- src/parser.ts` returns a single commit, 4c1e2f9.
**Selects a full commit identity:** git rev-parse 4c1e2f9 prints the 40-character hash for the report.
**Uses show to inspect that commit's exact patch:** git show will display the added `if (!input) throw` line and its message.
examples.result: The learner names the right commit, with the patch as evidence, instead of blaming the newest one.

examples.title: Finding when a feature appeared
examples.situation: A teammate asks when dark mode was added. The file theme.css has 60 commits.
walkthrough: git log --grep "dark mode" --oneline finds three candidates by message.
git log -S "prefers-color-scheme" confirms which one added the code.
git show --stat on it lists every file the feature touched.
examples.result: The answer comes with a date, author and patch, not a guess.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The newest log entry is always the commit that introduced a particular line or behavior.
misconceptions.correction: Later commits may only touch nearby code. Search for the specific text or behaviour with -S or blame, then confirm with git show.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Who changed the parser?", what did the newest commit actually change?

analogy.example: git log is **a library catalogue**: you filter by author, subject or keyword to get a shortlist. git show is **taking one book off the shelf and reading it**. Neither rearranges the library.
limitations: Catalogues list books; log can also search inside them with -S.
Books keep their exact identity number (hash) forever.

remediation.explanation: Always go **narrow then prove**: filter log by path and text until one or two commits remain, then read each with git show before naming it.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "Finding when a feature appeared".

recap.summary: To locate and explain the commit that introduced a change, filter git log by path, message or code text, record the full commit identity, and inspect the exact patch with git show, remembering these commands only read history and the newest commit isn't automatically responsible.
